title: Teamwork Contract
text: Milestone 1 asks your team to draft a team work contract. Below is a Quarto template to start from. It is based on a contract a past MDS team wrote for their DSCI 524 group project.

title: Teamwork Contract
text:
How to use the template

Create a file named team-contract.qmd. The contract is fairly personal, so it does not need to be in your public project repository.
Copy the template below (the button at the top right of the block copies it) and paste it into team-contract.qmd.
Replace everything in [square brackets]. The template is a starting point, not a form: change, add or remove anything so it describes how your team will work. See Milestone 1 for what a contract could cover.
Render it to PDF from the terminal:
quarto render team-contract.qmd
This creates team-contract.pdf next to it. The template uses Quarto’s built-in Typst format, so you do not need LaTeX installed.
Upload team-contract.pdf to Gradescope with your Milestone 1 submission.

title: Teamwork Contract
text:
Template
---
title: "Team contract"
subtitle: "DSCI 522, group [NUMBER]"
author:
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 1]"
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 2]"
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 3]"
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 4]" # delete this line for a team of three
date: today
format: typst
---

## Expectations

The time expected for group members to work on DSCI 522
will be a maximum of [NUMBER] hours a week,
unless all the team members agree to lengthen the time expected.
If team members cannot complete their sections within the maximum hours,
members should give notice on Slack at least 24 hours before the group submission deadline
to see if work should be redistributed or if the expected time should be increased.

All submissions are expected to meet the criteria of the milestones
as set out in the instructions.
This includes making sure all scripts are working,
creating tests for all our functions,
and using proper grammar in written submissions.

## Meetings

Meeting times were established during the initial team meeting held on [DATE].
Meetings will be held [PLACE, OR ONLINE ON ...] at the following times:

- [DAY]: [TIME]
- [DAY]: [TIME] (if needed)

The group will have a second formal meeting during the DSCI 522 lab on [DAY] at [TIME].
All members are expected to attend the meetings.
If a member cannot make a meeting,
written notice must be given 24 hours before the meeting to discuss alternative options.

## Communication

All communication outside of the meetings will be through Slack or GitHub.
GitHub will be the primary communication tool for ideas, suggestions,
submitting work and reviewing work.
Slack will be the primary communication tool for informal communication
and scheduling meetings.

## Reviews

All members are expected to submit a pull request for their work
on the group project's repository on GitHub.com.
Members are expected to add teammates as reviewers,
so that every pull request is reviewed by another teammate.
Pull requests should be reviewed within [NUMBER] hours after creation.

## Roles

There are two roles team members will be responsible for each week:

1. Scribe:
    - Responsible for taking notes at the meetings and in-class lab sessions,
      and adding them as a GitHub issue.
    - Responsible for sharing all notes and in-class activities with teammates.
2. Proof-reader:
    - Responsible for doing a final check of the submission before the deadline,
      to make sure all requirements are satisfied.

Roles will be rotated each week, so that each team member does each role at least once.

## Deadlines

Deadlines for individual items will be assigned during meetings.
The proof-reader will review the work on [DAY]
and ensure that the final version is ready for submission,
and will create the required GitHub release.

## Breach of contract

Failure to follow the team contract will result in a three-step warning system:

1. A written Slack notice that outlines the violation of the team contract
   and reminds the member of the team contract's conditions.
2. A meeting to discuss the behaviour,
   after which the member writes an agreement to follow the team contract.
3. Reaching out to the lab instructor or TAs about the issues with the teammate.

title: Individual assignment 1
text:
This assignment will provide practice in the context of version control and will prepare you to collaborate on your group projects for this course. Follow the instructions listed below. You will be graded for completion.

Create a new public repository on GitHub.com named learning-about-version-control. Make sure the repository:

Includes a README.md that has a header that says “Learning about Version Control” and has your name listed as the author.
Is public








Importantgithub.com not https://github.ubc.ca/



Make sure you do this in your own personal public GitHub account. Do not make this in the UBC github.



Clone your learning-about-version-control repository to your local computer.
Create and resolve a merge conflict 😱!

On your remote version control repository, use the pen tool to add a line to the README that says “Solving merge conflicts is easy!”
On your local version control repository, edit the same line in the README that you just edited, but this time write “Solving merge conflicts is soooooo hard!”
Add and commit your local changes to the README.md, and the try to push the file so that you create the merge conflict.
Resolve the merge conflict on your local computer so that the line reads “Solving merge conflicts takes conscious effort, but I can do it!”. Take a screen shot while you are resolving the conflict to document you did this.
Push the local changes to your remote version control repository.

Create and accept a pull request!

Create a new Git branch on your local version control repository named opinions and switch to that branch.
Edit your README.md so that you add at least one sentence about what you like most about version control, and add at least one sentence about what you find most challenging/confusing/frustrating about version control (we all have opinions on this one…). Add and commit your changes to local version control.
Push the changes to the README.md that you made on the opinions branch to the remote repository on GitHub.com.
Visit GitHub.com and create a pull request to suggest that the changes on the opinions branch should be merged into the main branch.
Accept the pull request you opened to merge your changes from the opinions branch into the main branch.

Follow the instructions for submission on Gradescope. Enter the URL and your explanation into Gradescope directly, and upload the screenshot there: there is no PDF to make. You will submit:

title: DSCI 522: Data Science Workflows
text:
Data-rich projects can quickly grow out-of-hand and become irreproducible in the absence of deliberate effort at organization, tool choice, and process. This course will teach basic principles of sound data scientific workflows and will develop skills implementing them in appropriate state-of-the-art systems and languages (e.g., Python and R).

Learning Outcomes
By the end of the course, students are expected to be able to:

map a data analysis question to appropriate analysis
use a Git/GitHub to collaboratively work on a data analysis project
manage project software and environment dependencies using virtual environments and containers
write scripts and analysis pipelines for non-interactive data analysis
run literate coding documents non-interactively
automate data science workflows

title: DSCI 522: Data Science Workflows
text:
Deliverables
This is a project-based course. You will work in randomly assigned groups of three (or four, if needed) for the project milestones. There are also individual weekly assignments that act as stepping stones to the project milestones. Finally, because collaboration is so important in data science, we will be using a team work multiplier to adjust individual grades. A combination of peer evaluation and GitHub history will be used to evaluate this.






WarningLab attendance is mandatory



Students are expected to attend 100% of their scheduled lab hours and attendance will be taken at the beginning of each lab session. Students must make formal requests for academic concession in the event that they cannot attend a lab session by filling out this academic concession form and sending it to the course instructor. Applying for academic concession does not promise the granting of academic concession. Each application will be evaluated in the context of UBC’s Academic concession policy. Students missing more than 20% of the total scheduled lab hours for a course without having received an academic concession will receive a possible maximum course grade of 50% and an “F” standing for the course on the transcript. For all other policies, please see the general MDS policies.








NoteWeekly oral check-ins



Each week during lab, a member of the teaching team will have a short oral check-in (about 5 minutes) with you. Think of it as practice for a technical interview: we will ask you to walk us through part of your project, such as what a script does, how a test works, or why you made a particular design choice. These check-ins are not graded. They are a low-stakes chance to practice explaining your technical work out loud and to get feedback and help along the way.

title: DSCI 522: Data Science Workflows
text:
Policies

Academic Integrity
Academic integrity is a commitment to honesty, respect, responsibility, and accountability in academic work. It is foundational to teaching and learning and is a shared value of all members of the UBC community. In a project course, it also means being transparent with your teammates and the teaching team about how your work was produced.
Academic integrity in this course includes:

Submitting individual assignments that reflect your own understanding and intellectual contribution.
Contributing your fair share to your group’s project, and making sure your commits, pull requests, and reviews honestly represent the work you did.
Citing any code, text, or ideas you draw on from elsewhere (classmates outside your group, documentation, Stack Overflow, blog posts, generative AI tools, etc.), following the MDS program policy.
Respecting the licenses of any code, data, or other material you reuse in your project.
Following the generative AI policy below, including disclosing AI use for every deliverable.



Use of Generative AI
This course follows the MDS program’s Academic Integrity and Use of Generative AI policy. Assessment-specific instructions always take precedence over the general guidance below.
AI assistance is allowed. Generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Cursor) are a real part of modern data science workflows, and you may use them in this course to brainstorm, explain concepts, debug errors, or help write code and documentation. That said, this course is about building your own skills in version control, environments, containers, testing, and pipelines. We strongly encourage you to attempt the work yourself first, and to use AI to support your learning rather than replace it. A useful question to ask yourself is: is this tool helping me understand the problem, or is it doing the thinking I am here to learn to do?
Disclose your AI use. For every milestone and individual assignment, you must state whether generative AI was used, including when it was not. If AI was used, please share:

which tool(s) and model(s) you used;
which parts of the work they were used for, and how; and
the instructions you gave the tool, such as any system prompt or agent configuration file (e.g., CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/, .github/copilot-instructions.md), or, if you did not use one, a few representative example prompts.

For group milestones, please keep this disclosure in an AI_USAGE.md file in the root of your project repository and update it as the project evolves. For individual assignments, include the disclosure with your Gradescope submission. Disclosing AI use is not penalized, and it helps us give you useful feedback.
You remain responsible for everything you submit. Whether code was written by you, a teammate, or an AI tool, everyone in the group is responsible for its correctness, quality, and licensing. You should be able to explain what your code does, why it is designed that way, and how it fits into the rest of your project. Please do not merge code you have not read and understood.
A human opens every pull request. AI agents may help you write code, but a group member must review any generated changes and open, review, and merge pull requests themselves. Please do not let an AI agent push to your repository, open pull requests, or merge them on its own. Because GitHub history is used to evaluate teamwork, it should accurately reflect who did the work.
Communicate in your own words. When writing issues, pull request descriptions, code reviews, peer reviews, and team work reflections, please use your own words. AI may help with translation or grammar editing. Much of what you learn in this course comes from these conversations with your teammates.
Weekly check-ins. As described in Deliverables, the teaching team will have a short, ungraded oral check-in with each of you during lab every week, as practice for technical interviews. We may ask you to walk us through any part of your project, including code that was written with the help of AI. If someone is not yet able to explain work they contributed, we will follow up to better understand how the work was produced and to support their learning. Where needed, this may also include steps under UBC’s academic misconduct procedures.
Protect private information. Do not share confidential, private, or sensitive information with AI tools, including personal information about yourself, your teammates, or other students (for example, peer review content or team work reflections).
If you are unsure whether a particular use of AI is appropriate, please ask the teaching team before you submit your work.
Academic misconduct
Violations of academic integrity (i.e., academic misconduct) may lead to serious consequences. For more details, please see UBC’s Academic Integrity website, the Academic Calendar Statement on Academic Misconduct, and UBC’s guidance on Generative AI.
Parts of this AI policy are adapted from the earthaccess AI policy, which is based on the SciPy and SymPy AI policies.


General Program Policies

Please see the general and genAI use policies in MDS policies.
Please review General Lab Instructions
Check the MDS Rubrics for grading criteria.

title: Milestone 1
text:
ImportantFind your group



Please make sure you are in the right group with the right teammates! Check here.


In this course you will work in assigned teams of three or four (see group assignments on GitHub) to answer a predictive statistical/machine learning question using a publicly available data set that will allow you to answer that question. To answer this question, you will perform a complete data analysis in R and/or Python, from data import to communication of results, while placing significant emphasis on reproducible and trustworthy workflows.
Your data analysis project will evolve throughout the course from a single, monolithic Jupyter notebook, to a fully reproducible and robust data analysis project, comprised of:

a well documented and modularized scripts written in R and/or Python,
a data analysis pipeline automated with GNU Make,
a reproducible report powered by Quarto,
a containerized computational environment created and made shareable by Docker
a remote version control repository on GitHub for project collaboration, sharing, and documentation.

An example final project from past years can be seen here: Breast Cancer Predictor

title: Milestone 1
text:
Milestone 1 summary
In this milestone, you will:

Draft a team work contract
Set-up a public GitHub repository
Create an appropriate file and directory structure for a data analysis project
Add the data analysis as a literate code document (Jupyter or Quarto)
Ensure the computation environment reproducible through a virtual environment (e.g., conda or renv) - hint do this as you create the analysis, don’t wait until the end!

An example Milestone 1 that corresponds to our expectations from this year is here: Breast Cancer Predictor in Python 0.0.1

1. Draft a team work contract
This document will govern the working relationships on your team, and if done correctly, it should help you manage and resolve any issues that might arise when working in a group. Start from the teamwork contract template, based on a contract from a past data science project: copy it into a Quarto document, make it your team’s own, and render it to PDF.
A team work contract communicates how the group will work together. It includes details about the logisitics of working together, the expectations you have for each other, and how you plan to navigate conflicts.
Some aspects of the team work contract could be:

How will work be distributed in a fair and equitable way?
What are the expected work hours for the project?
How often will group meetings occur?
Will you have meeting agendas and minutes? If so, what will be the system for rotating through these responsibilities?
What will be the style of working?

Will you start each day with stand-ups, or submit a summary of your contributions 4 hours before each meeting? or something else?

What is the quality of work each team member expects from themselves and each other?
When are team members not available (e.g., evenings and Sundays because of family obligations).
And any other similar things that govern your working relationships.

Use this opportunity to use your prior knowledge/experience to improve your teamwork, communication, leadership, and organizational skills. You will need all of these for your capastone projects (and beyond)!

Note - this document is fairly personal and does NOT need to reside in your public GitHub.com repo. Instead you can prove that you created this by submitting a copy of it to Gradescope under the Milestone 1 assignment.



2. Set-up a GitHub repository
Fill out this survey to provide us your GitHub.com username:https://ubc.ca1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_5p4MY2OnARUImy2
After we add you to the UBC MDS organization on GitHub.com, set-up a public GitHub repository for your group under that organization being sure to add all team members as collaborators. Once you have decided on a project question and data set, make sure your repository has a name that is relevant to that question. Note: if you need to change the name of your project repository later, you can!
We are using github.com and public repositories because we will eventually be using some fancy tooling (e.g., GitHub Actions) in this project. For this to work, all your work for this project (including scripts) should be developed and live in this repository on GitHub.com. Additionally, this will help you build a portfolio of your work you can share with others.


4. Create an appropriate file & directory structure for a data analysis project
For this project, you are expected to follow the best practices we have learned about in regards to project directory and file structures. This should be reflected in your GitHub repository. Specifically for this milestone, please ensure that you include at least the following 7 files and directories in your project’s GitHub repository:

README.md
CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
CONTRIBUTING.md
data/
<analysis>.ipynb or <analysis>.qmd (give it a meaningful name!)
environment.yml & Conda lock files for each major operating system (or the corresponding renv files)
LICENSE.md

The description of each of them follows.
Note - You should push both the source analysis document (<analysis>.ipynb or <analysis>.qmd file) AND the rendered document (PDF or HTML). If you choose to render to HTML, please setup GitHub pages to serve your html documents so that it is easily readable in the repository and share its URL in the README of your GitHub.com repo.

i. README.md
In the main README.md file for this project you should include: - the project title - the list of contributors/authors - a short summary of the project (view from 10,000 feet) - how to run your data analysis - a list of the dependencies needed to run your analysis - the names of the licenses contained in LICENSE.md
Note - this document should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repo.


ii. CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
In an attempt to create a safe, positive, productive, and happy community, many organizations and developers create a code of conduct for their projects. A code of conduct in a Data Science project informs others of social norms, acceptable behaviour and general etiquette. It is more outward facing than the team work contract discussed above. We recommend Project Include for a comprehensive guide to writing an effective Code of Conduct.
At minimum, we believe that a good/effective code of conduct should include:

A Statement on diversity and inclusivity
Details on expected, and unacceptable behaviour
A list of consequences for unacceptable behaviour
A procedure for reporting and dealing with unacceptable behaviour


Sample Codes of Conduct:

idocde Coc
Python Community CoC
Tidyverse CoC
Pandas CoC
Vox Media CoC

Note - this document should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.



iii. CONTRIBUTING.md
It is a good practice to include information about how others, outside the core team, can contribute to your project somewhere in your repository. This is typically done as a separate file in the repository called CONTRIBUTING.md. Here are some examples of this file:

Altair
dplyr
Atom editor (very comprehensive)
AI fairness research paper

Note - this document should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.


iv. data/
The data directory should contain a copy of the downloaded data (it should get written there by code). An exception to this can be made if the data set is extremely large (> 100 MB per file). In such cases, please reach out to the instructional team to make an alternative plan.


v. analysis.ipynb / analysis.qmd
For this milestone, the analysis code and narration should be contained within a single literate code document (e.g., Jupyter notebook or Quarto document). This document should not actually be named analysis.***, but have a more descriptive title, related to the project title.


vi. environment.yml & conda lock files for the major operating systems (or the corresponding renv files)
Include the necessary files (e.g., environment.yml & conda lock files for the major operating systems) so others can reproduce your work on their machine.
Note - this document should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.


viii. LICENSE.md
License’s tell others how they may (or may not) use your work. We will learn more about licenses later in the course, and for now we recommend using an MIT license for the project code and a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) license for the project report. As long as your group agrees, these can be changed later in the course when you learn more about licenses. If you want to spend some time choosing different licenses now, we can recommend these two websites to help get you started:

https://choosealicense.com/
https://chooser-beta.creativecommons.org/




3. Add the data analysis as a literate code document
The content of this analysis project should be a narrated analysis that asks and answers a predictive or inferential question using a method you have already learned in MDS. For milestone 1, the code and analysis narrative should be contained within a single Jupyter notebook (e.g., .ipynb file) or Quarto document (e.g., .qmd file). The analysis narrative should be rich and correct, with the following sections:

Title
Summary
Introduction:

provide some relevant background information on the topic so that someone unfamiliar with it will be prepared to understand the rest of your report
clearly state the question you tried to answer with your project
identify and describe the dataset that was used to answer the question

Methods & Results:

describe in written english the methods you used to perform your analysis from beginning to end that narrates the code the does the analysis.
your report should include code which:

loads data from the original source on the web
wrangles and cleans the data from it’s original (downloaded) format to the format necessary for the planned classification or clustering analysis
performs a summary of the data set that is relevant for exploratory data analysis related to the planned classification analysis
creates a visualization of the dataset that is relevant for exploratory data analysis related to the planned classification analysis
performs classification or regression analysis
creates a visualization of the result of the analysis

note: all tables and figure should have a figure/table number and a legend

Discussion:

summarize what you found
discuss whether this is what you expected to find?
discuss what impact could such findings have?
discuss what future questions could this lead to?

References:

at least 4 citations relevant to the project (format is your choose, just be consistent across the references).


The analysis can be performed in either R or Python. The restrictions on the analysis methods and programming language are put in place to ensure that all group members can contribute equally to the project.
The data for the project should be publicly available, and clearly licensed to be shared and used openly on the internet. We strongly suggest you avoid using data sets where authentication is needed for access (e.g., Kaggle) as this adds another layer of complexity when making these projects reproducible.

Possible data set sources

City of Vancouver Open Data Portal
BC Data Catalogue
Government of Canada open data
GitHub repo of awesome public datasets
UCI Machine Learning Repository: Data Sets
tidytuesday data set
Google Data set search engine
fivethirtyeight R package (if you use this, see the note below!)

Note: if you choose a data set from the fivethirtyeight R package, you cannot copy their scientific question, visualizations or methods from the original FiveThirtyEight articles from where the data sets were first reported on. Finally, with the fivethirtyeight R package data sets, we want you to get practice reading them using the read_* functions in R or Python, so please use the versions of the data sets listed here: https://github.com/rudeboybert/fivethirtyeight/tree/master/data-raw



6. Ensure the computation environment reproducible through a virtual environment
For this project, we will eventually be making the computation environment reproducible through containerization with Docker. For milestone 1 however, we will start with using a virtual environment as our first step towards this. You can use either conda or renv for this. Be sure to include the necessary files so others can reproduce your work. Be sure to include documentation of how to use the environment with your project as well in the README.md file.

Note: if you choose to do a project that uses conda as the virtual environment tool, you are expected to share environment.yml and the conda lock files for each major operating system (Windows, Linux and Mac, and for Mac you should share the intel and ARM versions).

title: Milestone 1
text:
Expectations

Everyone should contribute equally to all aspects of the project (e.g., code, writing, project management). This should be evidenced by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and participation in communication via GitHub issues.
After the repository is set-up, each group member should work in a GitHub flow workflow; where they create branches for each feature or fix, which are reviewed and critiqued by at least one other teammate before the the pull request is accepted.
You should be committing to git and pushing to GitHub.com every time you work on this project.
Git commit messages should be meaningful. These will be marked. It’s OK if one or two are less meaningful, but most should be.
Use GitHub issues to communicate to their team mate (as opposed to email or Slack).
Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense. It doesn’t have to be complicated.
You should use proper grammar and full sentences in your README. Point form may occur, but should be less than 10% of your written documents.
